prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Why not write something for those who scratched out improbable livings here? Someone has managed to sow This broken field with stones, it appears, So someone’s scratching it still, Although that Japanese knotweed has edged The tilth. Two wasps in the child Attempt to catch sun on a rail of the bridge. The old local doctor has passed At almost a full decade past ninety. He never seemed depressed. Seventy now, if barely, I consider the field again: Someone will drag these rocks away But they’ll be back. The air smells like rain, Which is fine, the summer’s been much too dry. Nothing is left of the barn But some rusty steel straps in some nasty red osier. The stone fence still looks sound, But even there the knotweed steps over. Hadn’t I pledged an elegy To the old ones who worked here? You couldn’t claim They thrived, exactly, but maybe They likewise scented good wind full of rain, Lifted eyes above this old orchard To the cloud-darkened hills and found their support Somehow, somewhere. No matter, They kept going until they could go no more. The trees’ puckered apples have gathered A flock of birds, and as they alight, They’re full of unseasonable chatter, As if to say that all will be right. The old ones I promised a poem Must have said it too. It’ll be all right. I never knew them. They’re gone. I say it out loud, It’ll be all right. —Caledonia County, Vermont

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Why, Someone, This

outputs.L1:
Why not write something for those  
who scratched out improbable livings here?

Someone has managed to sow  
this broken field with stones, it appears,  
so someone is scratching at it still,  
although Japanese knotweed has edged  
the tilth.

Two wasps in the child  
attempt to catch the sun  
on a rail of the bridge.

The old local doctor has passed,  
almost a full decade beyond ninety.  
He never seemed depressed.

Seventy now, if barely,  
I consider the field again:  
someone will drag these rocks away,  
but they will be back.

The air smells of rain,  
which is fine—the summer has been much too dry.

Nothing remains of the barn  
but a few rusty steel straps  
among some nasty red osier.

The stone fence still looks sound,  
but even there, the knotweed steps over.

Hadn’t I pledged an elegy  
to the old ones who worked here?

You couldn’t claim  
they thrived, exactly, but perhaps  
they, too, scented a good wind full of rain,  
lifted their eyes above this old orchard  
to the cloud-darkened hills,  
and somehow, somewhere, found their support.

No matter.  
They kept going until they could go no farther.

The trees’ puckered apples have gathered  
a flock of birds, and as they alight,  
they are full of unseasonable chatter,  
as if to say that all will be right.

The old ones I promised a poem  
must have said it, too:  
It’ll be all right.

I never knew them.  
They are gone.

I say it aloud:  
It’ll be all right.

—Caledonia County, Vermont
outputs.L2:
Why not offer a few words for the people who once wrested unlikely livelihoods from this land?

The ruined field seems to have been planted with rocks, yet someone continues to work the soil, even as Japanese knotweed advances along its edge. On the bridge railing, two wasps near the child try to settle into the sunlight.

The longtime country doctor has died at nearly one hundred years old. He never appeared unhappy.

Now close to seventy myself, I look over the field once more. Someone may haul off these stones, but they will return. Rain is in the air, and that is welcome after such an overly dry summer.

The barn has vanished, leaving only rusted metal bands tangled among unpleasant red osier. The stone wall remains sturdy, though knotweed is climbing across it too.

Didn’t I once promise to compose a lament for the elders who labored here? It would be hard to say they prospered. Still, perhaps they also breathed in a favorable wind heavy with the scent of rain, looked beyond the aging orchard toward hills dimmed by clouds, and somehow discovered something that sustained them.

Whatever the source, they carried on until carrying on was no longer possible.

Small, shriveled apples have drawn a gathering of birds to the trees. As the birds land, they chatter with an energy unusual for the season, sounding as though they are insisting that everything will turn out well.

Perhaps the departed people for whom I meant to write also repeated those words: Everything will be all right.

I did not know them. They are no longer here.

Still, I speak the assurance aloud:

Everything will be all right.

—Caledonia County, Vermont
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on the generations of people who struggled to make a living from the rocky, unforgiving fields of rural Vermont. Their labor is still visible in the remnants of the landscape, but nature and time are gradually erasing those traces. Invasive knotweed spreads across the field and orchard, surrounds the ruins of the barn, and overtakes the old stone fence, suggesting that the land is reclaiming what people once tried to cultivate and control.

This process of disappearance is made more personal by the death of the elderly local doctor, as well as by the speaker’s awareness that earlier generations have already passed away. Now aging, the speaker recognizes that mortality is not merely part of the region’s history but an approaching reality in their own life. The fading structures and overgrown fields thus become reminders of both human endurance and inevitable loss.

Although the people who once inhabited this land may never have truly prospered, they persevered. They found hope, reassurance, and companionship in the landscape, especially in its changing seasons and unpredictable weather. Their survival depended not only on physical labor but also on a persistent belief that hardship could be endured. In the present, the lively chatter of birds revives that same spirit of resilience. Listening to them, the speaker repeats the simple, consoling conviction that “it’ll be all right,” turning the phrase into an affirmation of hope in the face of aging, death, and change.
outputs.L4:
The speaker looks out over an old Vermont farm and reads its history in the land. Stone walls cross the fields, their rocks hauled and fitted together by hands long vanished. A ruined foundation marks where a house or barn once stood, while rusted tools, collapsed fences, and cellar holes suggest the daily labor that sustained families through harsh seasons. These remnants testify not to an easy pastoral life, but to generations of persistence: clearing stubborn ground, tending animals, repairing buildings, storing food, and enduring winters that could undo months of work.

Nature has begun to reclaim what those people made. Invasive knotweed crowds the neglected edges, spreading over disturbed soil and concealing traces of earlier habitation. Trees rise in former pastures, roots loosen old walls, and rain and frost slowly break apart the farm’s structures. Even the weather seems less dependable than it once was. Familiar seasonal patterns have shifted, bringing unusual warmth, violent storms, or uncertain snow. The farm therefore appears caught between two kinds of loss: the disappearance of the human community that shaped it and the destabilization of the climate that once governed its rhythms.

As the speaker surveys these changes, the landscape becomes an elegy for the people who lived there. Their names and individual stories may be forgotten, yet their effort remains visible in every cleared slope and carefully placed stone. The ruins preserve both their ambition and their defeat. They worked as though the farm would continue, as though children and grandchildren would inherit the fields, but time has scattered the families and reduced much of their world to fragments. The speaker honors them by imagining the burdens they carried and recognizing how much courage ordinary survival required.

Yet the scene is not wholly mournful. The hills, woods, and fields endure even as their uses change. Birds move through the abandoned spaces with sudden energy, calling from hedges, lifting from the grass, and filling the air above the ruins. Their liveliness does not erase the past, but it prevents the farm from becoming merely a monument to failure. Life continues in forms the former inhabitants could not have planned or controlled.

The birds also offer the speaker a model of resilience. They respond to weather and loss not by denying danger, but by continuing to build, migrate, feed, and sing. Their presence suggests that hope need not depend on restoring the vanished farm exactly as it was. Hope may instead consist of remaining attentive to what survives, caring for what can still be protected, and beginning again despite uncertainty.

By the end, the ruined Vermont farm holds grief and consolation together. Its stones and foundations record exhausting labor, broken continuity, and the passing of generations. Its overgrowth and altered weather reveal that neither human work nor familiar seasons are permanent. Nevertheless, the enduring land and the birds’ vivid activity affirm that persistence is still possible. The past cannot be recovered, but its example can be carried forward: people may continue to work, remember, and hope, even when they know that everything they build is vulnerable to time.
outputs.L5:
### Why Someone Chose This

“Why?” is often the first question we ask when life surprises us. We want reasons, explanations, and a clear path through uncertainty. Yet answers do not always arrive when we need them.

Sometimes, someone enters our life and changes the way we see the world. They may stay for years or only for a moment, but their presence leaves a mark. Through them, we learn that not every connection must last forever to be meaningful.

Perhaps this is what matters most: accepting that life is made of questions, people, and moments we cannot fully control. We may never understand why someone made a certain choice or why this particular event happened. Still, we can choose to grow from it—and sometimes, that is answer enough.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse elegy set in rural Caledonia County, Vermont, reflecting on aging, vanished farmers, an overgrown field, and the stubborn hope that “it’ll be all right.”
counterfactuals.output:
In Caledonia County  
the hills keep their old counsel,  
shouldering spruce and weather  
above roads that frost heaves  
and April nearly takes.

The barn at the field’s far edge  
leans farther each year,  
its red gone inward—  
boards silvered like the hair  
of those who once forked hay there.

They are names now  
spoken at the store,  
at the diner before noon:  
men who knew each cow by her temper,  
women who could hear rain  
hours before it crossed Burke Mountain.

Their hands have left the gates.

Goldenrod crowds the pasture,  
milkweed lifts its pale lanterns,  
and young maples rise  
where the Jerseys grazed,  
thin as questions no one answers.

I walk more slowly than I did,  
stopping where the stone wall  
disappears under fern and blackberry.  
My knees predict weather.  
My memory opens and shuts  
like a warped door.

Still, beneath the burdock,  
the old field holds its furrows.  
Still, a rusted spring  
seeps cold into the grass.  
At dusk, one light comes on  
in a farmhouse across the valley,

small, yellow, steadfast.

Someone, carrying wood to the porch,  
pauses to look west  
where the clouds have broken  
over Wheelock and Walden.

Someone says to no one,  
or to the dead,  
or to the coming snow—

it’ll be all right.

And the dark, though unconvinced,  
makes room for the words.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemplative pastoral poem in the voice of a seventy-year-old speaker surveying an abandoned Vermont farm. Include stone walls, Japanese knotweed, signs of rain, birds in an old orchard, and memories of the people who once worked there.
counterfactuals.output:
**After Rain, on the Old Place**

At seventy, I walk more slowly now,  
as if the earth had asked me to attend  
to every stone the vanished farmers raised  
and fitted into walls along the hill.

Rain passed before me. In the ruts, its light  
lies trembling under alder leaves; the barn,  
gone silver at the hinges, gives off  
the dark, sweet breath of hay it cannot hold.

Japanese knotweed crowds the lower field,  
its hollow canes and white, late-summer flowers  
possessing what the scythes once kept in check—  
a green republic no one voted for.

Beyond it stands the orchard, bent with years.  
A chickadee works over a split limb;  
two robins quarrel where the apples fall,  
and cedar waxwings lift as one, then settle.

I knew the hands that pruned these stubborn trees:  
old Ezra, thumb worn smooth as harness leather;  
his wife, who called the cows through dusk and rain;  
their sons, red-faced, pitching the August hay.

All gone—their laughter with the threshing dust,  
their boots beside the stove, the kitchen lamp  
held yellow through November’s early snow.  
Even their names grow lichen in my mouth.

Still, water gathers in the cellar stones.  
Still, asters lean above the broken gate.  
The walls go on, though maples shoulder through,  
keeping no cattle, marking no one’s claim.

I rest my palm upon their patient gray  
and feel the cold rain hidden in the rock.  
What we abandon does not stay alone:  
roots enter it, and wings, and weathered light.

The farm is not restored, nor wholly lost.  
It dreams in thorn and apple, wall and weed.  
I stand within its silence, growing old,  
and hear the orchard filling up with birds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a modern New England poem about people who scratched out difficult livings from rocky land. Contrast decay and invasive plants with endurance, seasonal renewal, and quiet optimism.
counterfactuals.output:
**Stone Season**

They pulled a living from the hill  
one granite tooth at a time,  
stacked every refusal into walls  
that outlasted their names.

The cellar holes are green now.  
Barberry crowds the thresholds,  
bittersweet cinches the apple trees,  
and knotweed lifts its hollow canes  
beside the rusted milk stand.

Rain enters the old barn  
without knocking.  
Moss keeps the ledger.  
A fox sleeps where the stove once held  
a small red weather.

Still, each March, beneath the rot  
and last year’s burdock,  
maple roots begin their quiet work.  
Buckets shine along the road.  
Mud loosens the frost’s hard fist.

Someone resets a fallen stone.  
Someone prunes one surviving pear.  
At dusk, smoke rises straight  
from a house with patched clapboards,  
and in the field, dark with thaw,

the first green does not ask  
whether the land was ever kind.  
It comes up anyway—  
thin, stubborn,  
enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a place-based free-verse poem titled or ending with “Caledonia County, Vermont.” Let the speaker attempt an elegy for unknown rural ancestors while observing a ruined barn, a stony field, wasps, puckered apples, and cloud-darkened hills.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Caledonia County, Vermont**

The barn has fallen inward  
as if listening for a voice  
beneath its own weathered boards.

No names remain in the loft—  
only hay turned gray as mouse fur,  
a hinge rusted open,  
the long ribs of rafters  
holding a little rain.

I have come to mourn you,  
whoever you were:  
hands that lifted stone from stone,  
backs bowed into the grammar of winter,  
women carrying lamplight  
from room to room  
while the snow erased the road.

The field keeps what it knows.  
Its walls wander through sumac,  
each rock a stubborn syllable  
the earth would not swallow.

Wasps worry the eaves,  
gold-bodied, furious  
over their paper kingdom.  
In the grass, apples pucker  
on abandoned trees—  
small sour faces  
turned toward the house  
that is no longer there.

What can I give you  
but this late attention?

No psalm, no lineage,  
no dates cut cleanly in slate—  
only hills going dark  
under a burden of cloud,  
only the wind searching  
the broken stalls  
for the warmth of cattle.

If your blood is in me,  
it moves without a map.  
If your grief is mine,  
I have mistaken it for weather.

Still, I stand at the stone wall  
and speak into the thistle,  
into the hive and the ruined beams:

You were here.  
You endured what would not remember you.

Cloud-shadow closes the fields,  
and the cold comes down early  
in Caledonia County, Vermont.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a meditative, conversational poem about mortality and resilience on an old Vermont homestead. Mention a local doctor who lived past ninety, a speaker nearing seventy, an overly dry summer, approaching rain, and the repeated reassurance, “It’ll be all right.”
counterfactuals.output:
The stone wall has outlived three barns,  
two marriages, and every hired hand  
who swore he’d come back in the spring.

Dr. Hale, from down the road,  
lived past ninety—still making calls  
with his black bag and patient knock.  
He used to say, “The body knows  
a few things we don’t.”

I’m nearing seventy now,  
and some mornings the stairs  
seem steeper than the hill pasture.  
Still, I carry kindling, mend the gate,  
set another cup beside the stove.

It’s been an overly dry summer.  
The garden has gone gray at the edges,  
and the brook speaks mostly in stones.  
Even the old maples hold their leaves  
as if saving their breath.

But tonight the swallows fly low.  
Clouds shoulder over the western ridge,  
and the air smells dark and mineral.  
Rain is approaching—slow, certain,  
like a neighbor with time to sit.

“It’ll be all right,” I tell the beans,  
the roof, the ache in my left hand.  
“It’ll be all right,” the thunder answers,  
not promising forever,  
only this rain, this hour,  
the house still standing.

And perhaps that is enough:  
to be here when the first drops fall,  
to hear the earth receive them,  
to know what bends may rise again.

“It’ll be all right,” I say once more—  
not because I’m sure,  
but because the old fields listen,  
and because, for now,  
so do I.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
